title: Sun safety: simple daily habits that protect your skin
excerpt: Coimbatore sun is strong all year. Shade, clothing, hats, sunglasses and the right sunscreen — used together — protect your skin best.
body:
Most skin cancers are caused by too much ultraviolet (UV) light from the sun. UV light also causes sunburn, early wrinkles and dark spots — and it makes pigmentation problems such as melasma and acne marks harder to treat. Sun protection is not only for the beach: in a sunny city like Coimbatore, it matters every day of the year.

## When is the sun strongest?

UV rays are strongest from about **10 am to 4 pm**. The daily UV Index (shown in most weather apps) tells you how strong UV light is where you live — when it is **3 or higher**, protect your skin.

UV light still reaches you on **cloudy or cool days**, and it bounces off water, sand and cement, so you can burn even when you don't feel hot.

## Use several kinds of protection together

- **Shade:** stay under a tree, umbrella or shelter when you can — but shade alone is not enough, so combine it with the steps below.
- **Clothing:** long sleeves and long pants or skirts protect best. Tightly woven fabric blocks more light than loose weaves, and dry fabric protects better than wet.
- **A hat:** choose a wide brim that shades your face, ears and the back of your neck. A cap leaves the ears and neck exposed.
- **Sunglasses:** pick ones that block both UVA and UVB. Wraparound styles also block light from the sides.
- **Sunscreen:** use it on all skin that clothing does not cover.

## Using sunscreen properly

- Choose a **broad-spectrum** sunscreen (protects against UVA and UVB) with **SPF 15 or higher**. For long hours outdoors, many dermatologists suggest SPF 30 or more.
- Apply it **generously** — most people use too little — including the ears, neck and backs of the hands.
- **Reapply** if you stay in the sun for more than 2 hours, and after swimming, sweating or towelling off.
- Check the expiry date. Heat can shorten a sunscreen's life, so don't leave it in a hot car.
- Babies **6 months or younger** should not use sunscreen — keep them out of the midday sun and cover them with clothing instead.

## Avoid tanning

There is no such thing as a safe tan. Tanning — in the sun or in a tanning bed — means UV light has damaged your skin cells.

## When to see a dermatologist

Book a skin check if you notice a new spot, a mole that is changing, or a sore that does not heal. If you have pigmentation, acne marks or melasma, we can also suggest a sunscreen that suits your skin type.

## Source

Based on public health information from [CDC — Sun Safety](https://www.cdc.gov/skin-cancer/sun-safety/index.html).
author: THE MIRRORS DERMATOLOGY CLINIC

title: Skin cancer: the warning signs worth checking
excerpt: Most skin cancers can be treated successfully when found early. Learn the types, who is at risk and which changes need a doctor’s look.
body:
Skin cancer is the most common cancer in many parts of the world. The good news is that it is often visible on the surface of the skin — so you can notice changes early, and **treatment works best when skin cancer is found early**.

## The main types

- **Basal cell carcinoma** and **squamous cell carcinoma** are the most common. They usually appear on skin that gets a lot of sun — the head, face, neck, hands and arms.
- **Melanoma** is less common but more dangerous, because it can spread to other parts of the body if it is not treated.

## Who is at higher risk?

Anyone can get skin cancer, including people with brown or dark skin. Your risk is higher if you:

- spend a lot of time in the sun or have had sunburns
- have light skin, hair or eyes
- have a family member who has had skin cancer
- are over 50

## Changes to look out for

Check your skin once a month in good light, using a mirror for hard-to-see areas. See a dermatologist if you notice:

- a **new growth** or spot that looks different from the others
- a **mole that changes** in size, shape or colour, or has uneven borders
- a spot that **itches, bleeds or crusts**
- a **sore that does not heal** within a few weeks

In people with darker skin, melanoma can also appear on the **palms, soles, under the nails** or inside the mouth, so include these areas in your check.

## How it is diagnosed and treated

A dermatologist examines the spot, often with a magnifying tool called a dermatoscope. If it looks suspicious, a small sample (a **biopsy**) is taken and checked in a laboratory.

Treatment depends on the type and stage. Most early skin cancers are removed with minor surgery. Other options include radiation, photodynamic therapy (a medicine activated by a special light), chemotherapy and medicines that help the immune system fight cancer.

## Prevention

Sun protection is the best prevention: shade, protective clothing, a wide-brimmed hat, sunglasses and broad-spectrum sunscreen — and no tanning.

## Source

Based on public health information from [MedlinePlus — Skin Cancer](https://medlineplus.gov/skincancer.html) (U.S. National Library of Medicine) and [CDC](https://www.cdc.gov/skin-cancer/sun-safety/index.html).

title: Acne: what causes it and the treatments that work
excerpt: Whiteheads, blackheads, painful nodules — acne comes in many forms. Here is what drives it, what makes it worse and how dermatologists treat it.
body:
Acne happens when hair follicles (pores) become clogged with oil and dead skin cells. Bacteria that normally live on the skin then multiply inside the blocked pore and cause inflammation. It usually affects the face, but can also appear on the back, chest and shoulders.

Acne is most common in teenagers and young adults, but many people still have it in their thirties, forties and even fifties.

## Types of acne spots

- **Whiteheads** — clogged pores that stay under the skin
- **Blackheads** — clogged pores open at the surface. The dark colour comes from air reacting with the oil, **not from dirt**.
- **Papules** — small, pink, tender bumps
- **Pustules** — bumps with white or yellow pus on top
- **Nodules and cysts** — large, deep, painful lumps that are most likely to scar

## What causes it?

- **Hormones** — rising hormone levels during puberty, around periods or in pregnancy increase oil production
- **Family history** — acne often runs in families
- **Some medicines** — including certain hormones, steroids and lithium

**Stress, humidity, pollution, tight helmets or straps, and picking or scrubbing** do not cause acne, but they can make it worse.

## How dermatologists treat acne

Treatment is chosen according to the type and severity of your acne:

- **Creams and gels** — benzoyl peroxide, retinoids (vitamin A-based), topical antibiotics, salicylic acid
- **Tablets** — antibiotics for moderate to severe acne, hormone therapy for some women, and isotretinoin for severe or stubborn acne
- **Procedures** — chemical peels, steroid injections for painful nodules, and treatments for scars such as microneedling and fillers

Acne treatments take time — usually several weeks before you see a clear change — so follow your plan consistently.

## Daily skincare tips

- Wash gently with a **mild cleanser** twice a day and after sweating; rinse with lukewarm water
- Use **oil-free, non-comedogenic** makeup, sunscreen and hair products
- **Don't squeeze or pick** — it can leave scars and dark marks
- Avoid harsh soaps, astringents and rough scrubs
- Use **sunscreen daily** — in brown skin, acne often leaves dark spots, and sun makes them darker

## When to see a dermatologist

See us if your acne is painful, leaving scars or dark marks, affecting your confidence, or not improving after a few months of over-the-counter products.

## Source

Based on public health information from [NIAMS — Acne](https://www.niams.nih.gov/health-topics/acne) (U.S. National Institutes of Health).
author: THE MIRRORS DERMATOLOGY CLINIC

title: Eczema (atopic dermatitis): calming the itch and preventing flares
excerpt: Eczema makes skin dry, itchy and inflamed. It can’t be caught from others — and the right daily care keeps most flares under control.
body:
Atopic dermatitis — the most common type of eczema — is a long-lasting condition that makes the skin dry, red, itchy and inflamed. It tends to come and go: **flares** when it gets worse, and quieter periods when the skin improves. It is **not contagious**.

## Symptoms

The main symptom is **intense itching**. Scratching then causes more redness, swelling, cracking, oozing and thickened skin. Where it appears depends on age:

- **Babies** — face, scalp and around the joints
- **Children** — inside the elbows and knees, neck and ankles
- **Teens and adults** — hands, neck, eyelids, ankles and feet

On brown and dark skin, eczema patches may look **darker or lighter** than the surrounding skin rather than red.

## Who gets it?

It usually starts in infancy or childhood and often improves before the teenage years, but adults can get it too. It is more likely if family members have eczema, asthma or hay fever.

## What triggers flares?

In eczema, the skin's protective barrier is weaker, so moisture escapes and irritants get in. Common triggers include harsh soaps and detergents, perfumes, cigarette smoke, rough fabrics such as wool, overheating and very dry skin.

## How it is treated

- **Moisturisers** to repair the skin barrier — the foundation of every treatment plan
- **Steroid creams** to reduce inflammation during flares
- **Non-steroid creams** (calcineurin inhibitors and others) for sensitive areas or long-term control
- **Light therapy** for widespread eczema
- **Newer tablets and injections** (JAK inhibitors and biologics) for severe eczema
- **Antibiotics** if the skin becomes infected

## Daily care that really helps

- Take **one lukewarm bath or shower a day** with a mild, fragrance-free cleanser
- **Pat** the skin dry and apply moisturiser within a few minutes, while the skin is still slightly damp
- Prefer **thick creams or ointments** over thin lotions
- Wear soft cotton clothes and keep nails short to limit damage from scratching
- Keep a routine — eczema care works best when it is done every day, not only during flares

## When to see a dermatologist

See us if the itch is affecting sleep, the rash is spreading, it is not improving with moisturisers, or you see signs of infection such as yellow crusts, pus, pain or fever.

## Source

Based on public health information from [NIAMS — Atopic Dermatitis](https://www.niams.nih.gov/health-topics/atopic-dermatitis) (U.S. National Institutes of Health) and [MedlinePlus — Eczema](https://medlineplus.gov/eczema.html).

title: Psoriasis: more than a skin condition
excerpt: Psoriasis causes thick, scaly patches when skin cells grow too fast. It can’t be cured yet — but today’s treatments control it very well.
body:
Psoriasis is a long-lasting condition in which an overactive immune system makes skin cells grow too quickly. The extra cells build up into **thick, scaly, inflamed patches**, most often on the scalp, elbows and knees. It is **not contagious**, and it affects men and women equally.

## Types of psoriasis

- **Plaque psoriasis** — the most common: raised patches covered with silvery scales
- **Guttate psoriasis** — small red spots, often in children or young adults, sometimes after a throat infection
- **Pustular psoriasis** — pus-filled bumps, usually on the hands and feet
- **Inverse psoriasis** — smooth red patches in skin folds
- **Erythrodermic psoriasis** — rare but serious redness and scaling over most of the body

## Symptoms

Itchy or burning patches, dry skin that cracks or bleeds, **thick or pitted nails**, and poor sleep. Like eczema, psoriasis comes in flares.

## It can affect the whole body

Some people with psoriasis develop **psoriatic arthritis** — joint pain, swelling and stiffness. Tell your doctor about any joint symptoms early, because untreated arthritis can permanently damage joints. Psoriasis is also linked with heart disease, diabetes, depression and other conditions, so regular health check-ups matter.

## What makes it worse?

Stress, skin injuries, infections, certain medicines, smoking, alcohol and excess weight can all trigger or worsen flares.

## Treatment

There is no cure yet, but treatment can clear or greatly reduce symptoms:

- **Creams and ointments** — usually steroids, vitamin D-based creams, retinoids or coal tar — for mild to moderate psoriasis
- **Phototherapy** — controlled ultraviolet light treatment for larger areas
- **Tablets** — such as methotrexate and other systemic medicines for moderate to severe psoriasis
- **Biologic injections** — target specific parts of the immune system for severe psoriasis

## Steps that help

- Moisturise daily with a thick cream, ideally right after a lukewarm bath
- Keep a healthy weight, stop smoking and limit alcohol
- Learn your triggers and avoid them where you can
- Ask your doctor before using sunlight as treatment — small amounts may help, but sunburn can trigger a flare

## When to see a dermatologist

See us if you have scaly patches that keep coming back, nail changes, a rash on the scalp that dandruff shampoo doesn't fix, or joint pain with skin symptoms.

## Source

Based on public health information from [NIAMS — Psoriasis](https://www.niams.nih.gov/health-topics/psoriasis) (U.S. National Institutes of Health).

title: Vitiligo: facts, myths and treatment options
excerpt: Vitiligo causes white patches when the skin loses its colour cells. It is not contagious — and treatment can stop it spreading and bring colour back.
body:
Vitiligo is a long-lasting condition in which the immune system attacks **melanocytes** — the cells that give skin its colour. This leaves **white or lighter patches** of skin. It is common, it can start at any age (often before 20), and **it is not contagious** — it cannot spread by touch, food or sharing things.

## Signs of vitiligo

- Pale or white patches, often on the **hands, feet, arms and face**, but they can appear anywhere
- **White hair** in affected areas — on the scalp, eyebrows, eyelashes or beard
- Loss of colour inside the mouth or nose

Most often the patches appear on **both sides of the body**. A less common type, **segmental vitiligo**, affects only one area or one side, usually starts young, spreads for 6 to 12 months and then often stops.

## What causes it?

Vitiligo is an **autoimmune** condition, and it can run in families. It is more common in people with other autoimmune conditions such as **thyroid disease**, type 1 diabetes, psoriasis, rheumatoid arthritis or lupus. Sunburn, emotional stress or contact with certain chemicals can sometimes trigger or worsen it.

## How it is diagnosed

A dermatologist examines the skin, often using a **Wood's lamp** (a special ultraviolet light) under which vitiligo patches glow chalky white. Blood tests for thyroid and other autoimmune conditions may be advised.

## Treatment options

There is no permanent cure yet, but treatment can **stop vitiligo from spreading** and **bring colour back** to many patches. Results take time and vary between body areas.

- **Creams** — steroids or calcineurin inhibitors
- **Phototherapy** — light treatment for larger areas, and targeted lasers for small patches
- **Surgery (skin grafting)** — for stable vitiligo that hasn't responded to other treatment; not done while patches are still spreading
- **Depigmentation** — lightening the remaining skin, considered only when vitiligo covers most of the body

## Looking after your skin

- **Protect patches from the sun** — they have no natural protection and burn easily. Use sunscreen and cover up.
- Camouflage makeup can cover patches if you wish — ask your doctor which products are safe.
- Living with vitiligo can be emotionally hard. Talking to family, a support group or a counsellor helps.

## When to see a dermatologist

See us early when you notice a new white patch — treatment works best when vitiligo is treated before it spreads. A dermatologist can also confirm whether a light patch is vitiligo or another, unrelated condition.

## Source

Based on public health information from [NIAMS — Vitiligo](https://www.niams.nih.gov/health-topics/vitiligo) (U.S. National Institutes of Health).

title: Alopecia areata: sudden round patches of hair loss
excerpt: Coin-sized bald patches that appear suddenly are often alopecia areata. Here is what causes it, whether hair grows back and how it is treated.
body:
Alopecia areata is a condition in which the immune system attacks hair follicles, causing hair to fall out. It usually shows up as **one or more smooth, round bald patches**, often about the size of a coin, on the scalp or beard. Most people with it are otherwise healthy.

## Signs to look for

- Hair loss that starts **suddenly**, on the scalp, beard, eyebrows or eyelashes
- Smooth bald skin with **no rash, redness or scarring**
- Short broken hairs at the edge of the patch that narrow at the base ("exclamation mark" hairs)
- Sometimes tingling, burning or itching just before the hair falls
- Small **pits in the nails**

## Types

- **Patchy alopecia areata** — the most common type, with one or more round patches
- **Alopecia totalis** — loss of all or nearly all scalp hair
- **Alopecia universalis** — rare loss of hair across the scalp, face and body

## Who gets it and why?

Anyone can get it, most often in the teens, twenties or thirties. It is more likely if a close relative has it, or if you have thyroid disease, vitiligo, eczema or allergies. Stress or illness can trigger it, but often no clear trigger is found.

## Will the hair grow back?

Often, yes. Hair may **regrow on its own within a few months** — sometimes white or grey at first before its usual colour returns. New patches can appear while others regrow, and some people have repeated episodes. Regrowth is more likely when hair loss is limited.

## Treatment

Treatment aims to calm the immune attack on the hair follicles and speed up regrowth:

- **Steroid injections** into the patches — commonly used for patchy hair loss
- **Steroid creams or lotions**, and other medicines that act on the immune system
- **JAK inhibitor tablets** — a newer option for severe alopecia areata in adults

Many people with small patches need no treatment at all. Wigs, hairpieces and cosmetic options are also choices for some people.

## When to see a dermatologist

See us if you notice a bald patch, especially if it is growing or new patches appear. A dermatologist can confirm the cause — hair loss has many causes, and they are treated differently — and check for related conditions such as thyroid disease.

## Source

Based on public health information from [NIAMS — Alopecia Areata](https://www.niams.nih.gov/health-topics/alopecia-areata) (U.S. National Institutes of Health).
author: THE MIRRORS DERMATOLOGY CLINIC

title: Rosacea: facial redness, bumps and how to calm them
excerpt: Flushing, redness and pimple-like bumps on the cheeks and nose may be rosacea. Learn the triggers and the treatments that help.
body:
Rosacea is a long-lasting inflammatory skin condition that mainly affects the **cheeks and nose**. It comes and goes in flares. It is most common in middle-aged adults and in women — and in brown skin the redness can be harder to see, so rosacea is often missed.

## Symptoms

- **Flushing** that starts to stay — persistent facial redness, sometimes with burning or stinging
- **Acne-like bumps and pimples** (but without blackheads)
- **Small visible blood vessels** on the cheeks and nose
- **Thickened skin**, especially on the nose (mostly in men)
- **Eye symptoms** — dry, gritty, red or sore eyes and styes (ocular rosacea)

Eye symptoms need prompt attention, because untreated eye rosacea can damage the eyes.

## What causes it?

The exact cause is not known. Skin sensitivity, ultraviolet light, tiny organisms that live on the skin and your genes may all play a part.

## Common triggers

Keeping a short diary of flares helps you find your own triggers. Common ones include:

- sun exposure and heat
- emotional stress
- hot baths and intense exercise
- spicy food and very hot drinks
- alcohol
- strong wind and extreme temperatures

## Treatment

There is no cure, but rosacea can be controlled well. Improvement is gradual and can take **three months or more**.

- **Creams and gels** that reduce redness and bumps — usually the first step
- **Tablets** (certain antibiotics and other medicines) for moderate to severe rosacea
- **Lasers and intense pulsed light** to fade visible blood vessels and persistent redness
- **Eye drops** and gentle eyelid care for eye symptoms

## Gentle skincare for rosacea

- Use a **mild cleanser** made for sensitive skin and moisturise daily
- Avoid scrubs, exfoliants and alcohol-based products
- Use a **broad-spectrum sunscreen, SPF 30 or higher, every day**

Rosacea is easy to confuse with acne, and some acne products make it worse — so a proper diagnosis matters.

## When to see a dermatologist

See us if your face stays red, burns or stings, has bumps that don't respond to acne treatment, or if your eyes are often red and irritated.

## Source

Based on public health information from [NIAMS — Rosacea](https://www.niams.nih.gov/health-topics/rosacea) (U.S. National Institutes of Health).

title: Hives (urticaria): itchy welts and when to worry
excerpt: Hives are raised, itchy welts that come and go. Most clear up on their own — but swelling of the lips, tongue or throat is an emergency.
body:
Hives — also called **urticaria** — are raised, red or skin-coloured welts that itch. They often move around: a welt may fade within hours while new ones appear elsewhere. Hives are very common, and most people have them at least once in their life.

## What causes hives?

Hives happen when the body releases chemicals (such as histamine) that make the skin swell. Common causes include:

- **Allergic reactions** to medicines or foods
- **Infections**, including common viral infections
- **Stress**
- **Physical triggers** — cold, exercise, pressure on the skin or sunlight
- **Insect bites and stings**

People who already have allergies are more likely to get hives. Often, though, no single cause is found.

## Short-term and long-lasting hives

- **Acute hives** last less than six weeks and usually go away on their own.
- **Chronic hives** keep coming back for more than six weeks. They are usually not caused by an allergy, and they need a doctor's assessment and a treatment plan.

## Treatment

- Mild hives may need no treatment and fade on their own.
- **Antihistamine tablets** relieve itching and reduce new welts — your doctor will advise which one and how long to take it.
- Severe or long-lasting hives may need other prescription medicines.
- Avoid known triggers, wear loose cotton clothes and use cool compresses for the itch.

## When it is an emergency

Hives can sometimes come with **angioedema** — deeper swelling of the lips, eyes, tongue or throat. **Get emergency help immediately** if you have:

- swelling of the tongue, lips or throat
- difficulty breathing or swallowing
- dizziness or fainting

## When to see a dermatologist

See us if hives keep coming back, last more than a few days, affect your sleep, or you want to find out what is triggering them.

## Source

Based on public health information from [MedlinePlus — Hives](https://medlineplus.gov/hives.html) (U.S. National Library of Medicine).

title: Dandruff and itchy scalp: causes and what helps
excerpt: Flaking and itching are usually dandruff — but psoriasis, fungal infection and other conditions can look similar. Here is how to tell and what to do.
body:
Dandruff makes the scalp shed **white or yellow flakes**, often with itching. It usually starts after puberty and is more common in men. It is not caused by poor hygiene, and it is not contagious.

## What causes dandruff?

Most dandruff is a mild form of **seborrheic dermatitis** — a common condition that can also cause redness and irritation, and can affect the eyebrows, sides of the nose, behind the ears and the chest. It often gets worse with stress, in humid weather and when hair is washed less often.

In babies, the same condition appears as **cradle cap** — greasy, yellowish crusts on the scalp. It usually clears on its own within a few months; washing daily with a mild baby shampoo and gently brushing with a soft brush helps.

## Conditions that look like dandruff

- **Scalp psoriasis** — thick, red, scaly patches with silvery scale, sometimes beyond the hairline. About half of people with psoriasis have it on the scalp.
- **Ringworm of the scalp (tinea capitis)** — a fungal infection, mostly in children, causing itchy, scaly patches and **patches of hair loss**. It needs prescription treatment and can spread to others.
- **Contact dermatitis** — itching and redness after a new hair dye, oil or product.

## What helps

- Use a **medicated anti-dandruff shampoo** — common active ingredients include ketoconazole, zinc pyrithione, selenium sulfide, salicylic acid and coal tar.
- Leave the shampoo on the scalp for **a few minutes** before rinsing, so it has time to work.
- Use it 2–3 times a week until the flakes settle, then once a week to keep them away.
- Heavy hair oils can make seborrheic dermatitis worse for some people.

## When to see a dermatologist

See us if flakes and itching continue after a few weeks of anti-dandruff shampoo, if the scalp is very red, sore or thickly scaled, or if you notice **hair loss or patches** — especially in a child.

## Source

Based on public health information from [MedlinePlus — Dandruff, Cradle Cap and Other Scalp Conditions](https://medlineplus.gov/dandruffcradlecapandotherscalpconditions.html) (U.S. National Library of Medicine).
